He knows his statement is fallacious and misleading to the highest degree.
I refer Your Honour to standing order 41 and for your reference I quote paragraph 297 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, as follows:
The imputation of bad motives, or motives different from those acknowledged, misrepresenting the language of another, or accusing him, in his turn, of misrepresentation, charging him with falsehood or deceit; or contemptuous or insulting language of any kind; all these are unparliamentary and call for prompt interference.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 29, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the following question:
Mr. Speaker, is the government aware of the action taken recently by the medical profession of the city of Winnipeg with respect to medical services formerly afforded families on relief? If so, in the event of other means failing, will they intercede on behalf of these people and see that they are afforded proper medical services.
I received this answer from the Prime Minister:
Mr. Speaker, representatives of the medical profession met me in Ottawa some weeks ago, and later a communication was sent to them indicating that there was no reason to believe that the provinces would not discharge their constitutional duties with respect to the health of their citizens. subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the advisability of nationalizing life insurance.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in moving this
resolution I would like at the outset to make it clear to the house that my object is not particularly to criticize our Canadian life insurance companies nor the foreign companies doing business in Canada. That is to. say I have no reason to suspect that these companies are not carrying on their business as efficiently and also as safely as such companies are anywhere in the world. So I

Lije Insurance-Mr. Irvine
hope the discussion that may ensue will centre upon the question whether or not the business of life insurance in Canada could be done more efficiently and more cheaply for the people through the agency of the government than by private companies. In answering that question we have to ask what life insurance is for. What is the main consideration? Is it to keep the life insurance companies going? Is life insurance carried on in Canada for the purpose of collecting enormous funds in the hands of individual companies for investment? Or is not the object rather to provide protection for the people of Canada who need insurance? In this connection Judge Louis D. Brandeis, in commenting on an investigation carried on into the operations of life insurance companies in the United States, said:
The business is carried on for the benefit of others than the policyholders. The needs and financial inexperience of the wage^earner are exploited for the benefit of wage-holders or officials. The results establish conclusively that, in the conduct of the business, the interest of the insured are ignored.
That was the comment of a judge summarizing the evidence that had been put before a special investigating committee with regard to life insurance companies in the United States, and I am reasonably sure that, if there were to be a similar investigation in Canada such a comment would prove applicable to our own companies.
Life insurance is essentially social in character. In fact it is its social character that makes it possible. Further, because of its social character it is, unless it is tampered with, the safest business in the world. In the last analysis it really means that all the individuals embraced in one insurance company undertake together to protect one another to a given amount against the risks of mortality. There are always more policy-holders remaining than the number who die, and unless the funds of the contributors are misspent or badly invested there is no doubt about the safety of the business.
We have to ask then, with regard to our insurance companies in Canada, whether or not they are carrying out the chief function of life insurance, which is to insure the people. Or is the emphasis being placed principally on the success of the companies from a business point of view? Are there people in Canada to-day who are not insured who ought to be insured, and are they not insured because the price of insurance is too high? Then is it or is it not sc that the cost of insurance to the people of Canada who are insured is so high as to be a great burden upon many, so that under pressure of a depression such as we are
passing through large numbers are compelled to yield up their insurance, either by taking its cash surrender value or by letting it lapse and losing it entirely? Do these things not indicate, if they are as suggested, that the price of life insurance is too high to those who are insured, and prohibitive to those who are not?
Many people in Canada are not insured today, and I think it can be shown that those who are insured are paying much more for their insurance than should be necessary or would be necessary under a government scheme. Life insurance as carried on by the private companies is fairly successful, for those who can afford it, but there are many people who cannot afford it, and those are the people who need it most. The classes of people who need life insurance most in Canada obviously are poor people with large families, and those who may be regarded as poor risks, who either are not accepted at all by the companies or else the price is so high as to be prohibitive.
Let us look for a moment at the number of policies in force in Canada at the end of 1932. I find the number to be:
Industrial policies	 4,097,592
Ordinary policies	 2,487,691
Total	 6,585,283
In 1931 the total number of parsons in Canada fifteen years of age and over Was 7,095,571. It is common knowledge, I think, that in ordinary life insurance one individual may have a number of policies, two or three or in fact many in some instances. So while under the ordinary insurance classification we have 2,487,691 policies it is altogether likely that this does not mean that more than a million or so people are insured, because each indivdual thus insured probably will average about two policies. Moreover it must be remembered that in connection with industrial insurance a great number of childnen -are insured, and these are included in that four million. So if we take into consideration the number of children insured under industrial policies and the duplication of policies which we find under the other classifications of insurance, it is very doubtful if the number of people insured in Canada is greater than about half the number of people who require insurance. In other words I would say that about half the people of Canada who need insurance have no insurance at all. I do not think hon. members of this house will seriously dispute my contention when I say that the high cost of insurance, under our private insurance companies, makes it difficult for most of our people to get any insurance at all, and in fact if is impossible in many oases
Life Insurance-Mr. Irvine

The total number of companies doing business in Canada is some 62. In 1932 there were 43 active companies, 28 Canadian, 6 British and 9 foreign. In addition to those active companies there were six British companies and five foreign companies registered to transact life insurance but which have practically ceased to write new insurance, their business being confined to the policies already on their books, eight companies, four British and four foreign, were authorized under the act to transact business in connection with policies written prior to March 31, 1878. So there are forty-three active companies in Canada and sixty-two companies doing business to some extent.
I found some difficulty in getting information as to the Salaries paid the chief officials of the Canadian companies. The note from the department of insurance states that the managers do not constitute a well-defined class, that the officials and employees designated as managers in some companies are known by other designations in other companies. In the annual report of the department the total of head office and branch office salaries were given, from which the following figures have been compiled. For the year 1932 head office salaries of Canadian companies amounted to $10,089,615; for British companies doing business in Canada to $240,271, and for foreign companies doing business in Canada to $1,144,935, thus making a total head office salary account for all the companies doing business in Canada of $11,474,821. Then for branch office salaries, those of Canadian companies amounted in 1932 to $9,677,859; for British companies, $220,311 and for foreign companies $3,165,306. So we have the total head office and branch office salaries amounting to $24,538,297.
In passing we might note the enormous amount of money tied up in head office buildings. In 1932 the amount tied up in head offices in connection with Canadian companies was $39,359,124 and in connection with British and foreign companies $3,473,345, making a total of $42,832,469. Is it reasonable to bury $42,832,469 in head office buildings while hundreds of thousand of our people have no insurance?
The salaries of insurance executives are perhaps among the highest in the country, both in Canada and in the United States. The president of the United States and the ten members of his cabinet receive a total of $225,000 a year. The eleven highest paid officials in the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company received, in the depression year

1931, more than three times as much as was paid the president and cabinet of the United States; in other words, they received $684,000. This company has on its payroll 39 officers receiving salaries greater than the members of the cabinet receive. Three other companies paid their eleven highest paid officials more than twice as much as the president and his cabinet received. The New York Life Insurance Company paid their officials $604,800 and the Prudential Insurance Company $544,000.
In this connection I might just mention the salaries which are paid some of the officials of United States companies, many of which do business in this country. I am sorry I have not the actual figures in this connection for Canadian companies. First there is the Equitable Life Assurance Society; in 1929 the salary of Mr. T. I. Parkinson, president, was $75,000 per year, but that was increased so that in 1932 he received $100,000 per year. I think in the same company there are about four vice presidents who receive about $40,000 annuallly. Mr. F. H. Ecker, president of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, received $175,000 a year in 1929, which was later increased so that in 1932, during the depression, he received $200,000 annually. There are two or three vice-presidents in that company, one of whom receives $125,000 annually, another $40,000 and another $35,000. In the Mutual Life Insurance Company the president, D. F. Houston, received $100,000 per year in 1929, and later that was increased so that in 1932 he received $125,000. Mr. T. A. Buckner, president of the New York Life Insurance Company, received $100,000 in 1929 and $125,400 in 1932. Mr. E. J. Duffield, president of the Prudential Insurance 'Company of America, received $125,000 in 1929 and the same in 1932; his salary did not increase with the depression. I think these figures indicate that there is no need for us to be disturbed about the wellbeing of those who are in charge of some of our insurance companies.
A few years ago the state of New York made certain investigations as to the cost of acquisition of new insurance by the different companies. Again I have been unable to get the figures accurately for Canada, but in a moment I shall give them as I have them here.

speechtext:
These are the total lapses for the two main divisions of insurance, namely ordinary and industrial, for the years 1930, 1931 and 1932. These figures, I believe, tell a really tragic story when we stop to consider the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who, perhaps for years, have been trying to protect their families but during the past few years have had to release their hold and lose all that they had paid.
Let me now compare the only state insurance scheme concering which I have been able to get figures, with the companies with which I have been dealing. The ratio of expenses to gross premiums for the first year policies in the Massachusetts system in 1929 amounted to only 9-17 per cent, whereas the average for all companies doing business in that state was 49-21 per cent. It ran as high as 78 per cent in the case of one company. Private companies doing business in Massachusetts had an expense ratio to all those premiums of 18-32 per cent for ordinary policies and 26-34 per cent for industrial policies. These were the figures based on all business done in 1929. In the case of the Massachusetts savings bank system, this ratio was only 4-63 per cent. According to the annual report for 1929 of the Massachusetts commissioner of insurance, by eliminating selling costs, advertising and high salaries, the Massachusetts savings bank life insurance system was able to sell insurance 26 per cent below private companies and more than 50 per cent below the commercial rates on the weekly premium plan. Detailed figures show that in some cases two years' protection in a private insurance company cost the insured five times as much as it would have done under the state scheme. Another instance is that of a holder of a twenty-year endowment policy, aged 30 at entry. In the case of a S250 policy, the net result at the end of two years showed a cost of $2.50 under the savings bank life insurance scheme as compared with a cost of $31.20 in the case of a private company. In this instance the policy holder paid more than twelve times as much for $250 protection in an industrial insurance company as he would have had to pay for insurance under state control.

I see that my time in running short and I must turn from these figures to urge an argument based thereon. I urge that the whole life insurance business of this country should be taken over by the government. It is obvious that in a forty minute speech one cannot give a detailed plan for the taking over of insurance companies, but I do not know of anything that could be taken over more easily. The entire paid-up capital of all insurance companies in Canada amounts to only $10,000,000, and this is S10,000,000 that they have no business to have. Insurance companies do not need capital of that sort; $10,000,000 of unneeded capital is only an added charge upon the policyholders. It serves no other function. If the government took over the business now done by private companies it would be in an even better position to meet the requirements of the policyholders than private companies are. If the will was present, I do not anticipate any difficulty in the government finding a proper, efficient and effective way of putting this scheme into effect.
Perhaps one of the greatest advantages in favour of a state scheme is the wider distribution of risk which is made possible. The wider spread that can be given to the risk, the lesser risk there is and the cost of insurance accordingly becomes less. We have but to take the idea which is exemplified so well in group insurance and apply it to a still larger group, say to seven million Canadian citizens. As the group is enlarged, the cost is decreased. Under the group insurance plan an insurance company can go into a factory and sign up a group of fifty men without medical examination. They know from their actuarial experience that it is quite safe. They are able to give insurance to the oldest man as cheaply as the youngest. If that can be done with a group of fifty, it can be done much more easily with a group of seven million. By making this a national business and spreading the risk out to seven million people we can reduce the cost of insurance to a fraction of what it is now costing under the competitive system, figures in regard to which I have just given.
The next point in favour of nationalization is the compulsory feature. I suggest that our national insurance should be compulsory, it should apply to every person in the state who reaches a certain age. This age can be fixed at fifteen, eighteen, or twenty, that is a matter of detail. The maximum and minimum of the policies is another detail which could be arranged. The compulsory feature would reduce greatly the cost of insurance. At present

Li]e Insurance-Mr. Gershaw
we have forty-three companies in Canada, each with a network of agencies across the dominion; there are forty-three head offices and branch offices of each company in almost every city, town and village. There is an enormous cost in getting business under these conditions. A compulsory system under state control would permit this business being obtained for practically nothing. With a national compulsory scheme permitting the spreading out of risks there would be a material reduction in the cost of insurance and it would be brought within the reach of millions of our people who are now unable to obtain protection in a private company.
Another point to 'be considered is the amount of insurance investments in relation to the national economy. Perhaps I have time to put on record the figures in connection with the investments of Canadian insurance companies which I obtained from the Department of Insurance. These figures are the book value of the assets as at December 31, 1932. The Canadian real estate assets were valued at $55,034,238; the nomCanadian at $3,303,321, making a total of $58,337,559. I have not the time to give the details of other assets, so I shall give only the totals. The total Canadian assets of the Canadian companies were valued at $1,015,253,376; the nonCanadian at $528,182,242, making a total of $1,655,104,037. The total investments of these companies amount to well up to two billions of dollars.
I am one of those who believe that the time has come when this country will have to exercise some control over investments. If the Canadian government should make such a decision in the near future it would be necessary for them to obtain control of this tremendous sum which, is now at the mercy, if I may say so, of these private companies. It is not too much to say that these private companies collect money from the people of Canada and then invest that money to the detriment of those who subscribe. Sometimes the investment may be safe enough but I am sure that very often it is made in enterprises which do not need further capital. Over capitalization causes a rise in prices of the commodity produced to the very people who have furnished the money for the investment. Let me give an example. When binders were made by hand they could be bought by the farmers of Canada at about $100, but when the machine production made it possible to stamp out hundreds almost like biscuits, they cost about $300 apiece. The rise
in price was due very largely to overcapitalization, and insurance companies have done their share of over-capitalization among industries both in this and in other countries.
I contend that a government cannot afford to allow an investment of two billion dollars to be made by these sixty-two private companies if there is to be any control of investment with a view to national policy. I sincerely hope that the day is not far distant when the government of this country will insist on planning its investments with a view to the national economy, and thus taking hold of insurance from that point of view as well as from the point of view of giving insurance to all of the people of Canada at the lowest possible price. Let me also point out that the nation really is in the insurance business, whether it wants to be or not, for when an individual dies and leaves his dependents unprotected, their care falls upon the community. The community must 'take care of those who are not protected by insurance whether i-t is in the insurance business or not. I submit that it is bad business for the community to pick up only those who are entirely incapable of protecting themselves and to allow the cream to Ibe skimmed off 'by the private insurance companies who take as policyholders those who are well able to pay for insurance, and who perhaps scarcely need it at all.

subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks on this very important subject, not because I feel at all competent to deal with it exhaustively, but because I believe that insurance is one of the weapons that can be used -in fighting poverty. We have poverty in this country from coast to coast. We have poverty that is an unsatisfied need for goods, side by side [DOT] with unemployment, which is an unused ability to produce goods. Every observer will admit that these are the two great tragedies of the present time. If we can get a system of social credits which will solve these problems, by all1 means we should do so, but if we cannot we should at least come to grips with these problems and not pass up any opportunity of making things a little better. The social consciousness of the people of this country has been deeply stirred by the distress which has been brought about.
Insurance should do three things: (1) It should encourage the non-thrifty to save; (2) it should make secure for the industrious the product of their thrift; (3) above all, it should give that sense of security, in
.	COMMONS
Life Insurance-Mr. Gershaw
fact, that actual security which would bring satisfaction and freedom from worry to those who otherwise would view the future with fear and dread.
With most of the insurance schemes the agriculturist has nothing to do. He is excluded from the Workmen's Compensation Act. He would likely be excluded from an unemployment insurance act. But if insurance could be brought within reach of the agriculturist a great service would be done and he then would have the opportunity of sharing in its benefits.
We realize that the insurance companies have stood up reasonably well under the stress and strain of the last four years of depression. We realize that the insurance companies persuade most of the people to take out insurance. It may be true that they are taking a cut for themselves of 20 to 25 per cent, but if they are looking after our interests we perhaps would not begrudge them that percentage.
I wish to go into some detail and try to make clear just how safe our insurance is at the present time. Insurance has become a tremendous-a powerful-institution in Canada. It has been said there are some forty-three companies actively engaged in business, twenty-eight Canadian, six British and nine foreign. The life insurance in force in this country is around six and a half billion dollars, and the total assets of the insurance companies are $1,632,528,293. Out of ten million people in Canada there are in force ordinary policies to the number of 2,487,691 and industrial policies to the number of 4,097,592. The ordinary policy averages $2,143, and the average industrial policy, $201. Of course, Canadian companies do business in many other countries in the world besides [DOT] Canada.
The report of the Superintendent of Insurance gives these interesting figures. It states that out of each $100 of income received by an insurance company, $61.32 goes in disbursements in assurance and annuity contracts; $14.50 in general expenses; $1.51 in taxes; 33 cents in dividends to shareholders; $7.06 in other expenses, and $15.28 carried to reserve.
We must also realize that insurance is largely based on three things-the mortality tables, investments, and premium income. The mortality tables are compiled with great care. They give exact information that can be obtained by the insurance companies who can thereby tell just what calls are likely to be made upon them within any given period of 
time. The companies have perhaps been getting the breaks in this regard lately because people are living longer than they formerly did, and it must be said that the insurance companies are doing their part to help prolong life. They are paying for periodical medical examinations and are broadcasting health knowledge in very many ways, as well as supporting hospitals and similar institutions.
When we turn to their investments, we find that the funds of Canadian companies are widely diversified. They have invested in dominion, provincial, municipal, foreign and industrial bonds, also in preferred and common stocks. They have gone in for such things as power, apartment blocks, railways, real estate, farm mortgages and so forth. Anyone looking over a list of these investments will realize that the securities of life insurance companies have in some cases depreciated very largely in recent years. Of course they have only a certain percentage of their funds in any one type of investment, but summing up the investment program we must conclude that the companies are reasonably well managed and can carry on so long as the normal growth of the nation continues. And it is on that assumption that the security of the policyholder rests.
Insurance companies have a continuous stream of money coming in as premium income. This is a very substantial amount. In 1932 for the ordinary life industrial policies in Canada there was received in premiums $137,029,051, with perhaps another $4,000,000 for group insurance. This has increased rapidly in recent years. In 1931 it amounted to $144,000,000. But in 1922 it was just $67,000,000; in 1912, $23,000,000; in- 1902, $10,000,000; in 1892, $4,750,000 in 1882, only $1,500,000.
This income has increased and it can continue to increase just so long as the volume of business increases, the population increases, the popularity of the insurance keeps up and the ability of policyholders to pay continues. From these sources insurance companies receive their returns and upon this security they are able to make their payments to policyholders. Therefore we must recognize these factors in estimating the strength of insurance companies.
During times past insurance was written on many different plans such as term insurance, endowment insurance, twenty pay life and so on, but recently I understand that the popular policies are life income, or refund annuity, and that our chartered companies are selling a great deal of insurance on this basis. It must be remembered that in years long gone

Lije Insurance-Mr. Rhodes
by the Dominion government established a system of government annuities and in so doing they provided for Canadian funds a place for investment which stands high to-day. My reason for rising now is to try to put forward the idea that by the use of this scheme as a framework, a policy could be worked out which would go a long way toward providing unemployment benefits and perhaps looking after the requirements of old age pensions. I know it is stated that rates for these annuities are too low; that they are based upon out-of-date mortality figures and that the government is paying all expenses of administration; but the fact remains that this stands out as one of the premium investments at the present time.
Let us take a few examples. Persons taking out annuities can start paying at any age; they can pay monthly or quarterly or yearly or, if they so desire, they can purchase their policy with a single payment, a single premium. If a man aged twenty wishes to have an income of $100 per annum after he

I understand it would perhaps not be advisable for the government to assist an optional, noncompulsory form of protection like this, but some other scheme could be worked out. For instance, the officers of the income tax branch know what income almost every person in Canada is receiving from wages or dividends. They could ask those who are paying income tax to pay a little more and thus get this protection. They could ask those who are not paying income taxes to contribute some of these small amounts that I have mentioned and thus make sure that their old age would be provided for. With this as a basis the government would be justified in contributing certain amounts, probably asking the industries to contribute certain sums and thus work out a scheme which would provide protection in case of unemployment or sickness, and perhaps for old age pensions at a younger age than that at which they start at the present time.
I believe along these lines something could be done to evolve a workable plan that would banish the spectre of poverty and want and along these lines the government could very well nationalize insurance.
Hon. E. iN. RHODES (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I had rather thought a subject of this importance would have received at the hands of the house more attention than is apparently indicated by the limited number of speeches we have had upon the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Wetaski-win (Mr. Irvine). At the outset of his remarks he said that he had no intention of criticizing insurance business, nor had he reason to think the business in Canada was not conducted as effectively and efficiently as in any other part of the world, but he very shortly afterwards followed that by a citation from, I take it, a decision of Judge Brandeis of the United States, whether he was sitting as a judge or a commissioner, I am not at the moment aware. At all events, the citation which he gave and which I was not able to take down owing to the rapidity with which my hon. friend speaks, was a criticism of the manner in which insurance business had been conducted in the republic to the south. Then he proceeds to say he is not sure that the same criticism might not be levelled against

Lije Insurance-Mr. Rhodes
the insurance business in Canada. I submit that the hon. member's reference to the statement of Judge Brandeis was hardly in keeping with the statement he made at the outset of his remarks; and that, even assuming that the criticism of Judge Brandeis was true with respect to insurance in the United States, it by no means follows that it is true with respect to insurance in Canada. I think that, by and large, we have reason to feel proud of the stupendous insurance business which has been built up in Canada, and, on the whole, of the character of that business and the manner in which it has been conducted. I think it compares favourably with any similar business to be found in any country in the world. While I am not suggesting for a moment that it is not capable of improvement-no human institution is perfect-I do say that on the whole it has served the people' of this country extremely well, and I deprecate any suggestion, emanating either from the resolution or from discussion in the house, that we have not full confidence in and reason to be proud of the manner in which insurance has been conducted in Canada.
My hon. friend cited some figures as to salaries paid to insurance executives in the United States. I have never heard criticism levelled against high salaries paid to insurance executives in Canada. I am prepared to admit that my personal feeling is that we have gone too far in many instances in the high salary field-

subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext:
I do not believe any man is worth the gigantic salaries paid to executives in some institutions, chiefly in other countries. On the whole we have been happily free from that tendency in Canada, with rare exceptions. But having said so much let me say this:
I have no doubt in the world you could get insurance executives for $1,000 a year. But they would be the most expensive men you could possibly get- It by no means follows that because you paj' an excessive salary to an executive, ipso facto the cost of insurance is going up. Even if salaries are excessive, the successful management of the business is of far more importance to those dependent upon it than the mere amount of the salary, which after all is but a trifling percentage of the amount involved in the business. It would be a mere fraction spread over the millions of policy-holders in a given company. If salaries of executives were eliminated altogether the effect on the dividends paid to 
policy-holders or the premiums collected would represent but a fraction of a cent. So my reference to that is merely to indicate that it has practically no effect upon the main result.

My hon. friend gave a multiplicity of figures. I do not propose to follow him in detail even if it were desirable, but I will cite a few figures which I think have an important bearing upon the manner in which we should approach the consideration of a resolution of this kind. I think perhaps my hon. friend will agree that perhaps one of the main essentials of life insurance is security, both for the business and for the policy-holders. In that connection I may point out ithat during the eighty-five years that life insurance has been in force in Canada under government supervision there has never been a dollar lost to a policy-holder. Furthermore, during .the past fifty years, dm which there has been government sujpervision of foreign companies doing business in this country, and deposits have been required as security for the fulfillment of insurance contracts, there has never been a dollar lost to a policy-holder through effecting insurance in any foreign company. Our records are complete with respect to insurance companies back to the year 1875, a period of fifty-eight years. That being so we must look into the question of the liabilities involved in case the Dominion of Canada were to determine to take over the life insurance business of existing companies. My hon. friend gave the paid up capital of insurance companies as $10,000,000. I would not for one moment suggest that my hon. friend would deliberately mislead the house, but he altogether failed to take into consideration the premiums which were paid on subscriptions to stock in insurance companies, which represent several millions. speechtext: All stolen from the policyholders.

speechtext: No, I do not subscribe to that point of view ait all.

subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext: I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext:
Not stolen from the policyholders at all. As a matter of fact under the law shareholders of insurance companies are entitled to take up to ten per cent of the earnings of the company. But voluntarily they have reduced that to five per cent, leaving the remaining ninety-five per cent available for the benefit of the policy-holders. Some companies have never taken full advantage of that five per cent; they have allowed substantial sums of money to appear as accumulated reserves for the policy-holders.
Assuming that it were desirable to take over the insurance business in Canada, what does it involve in the way of immediate commitment on the part of the dominion? As of December 31, 1928, the stocks of the Canadian insurance companies were selling at a market value of $94,000,000. I have no doubt that at once I will be met with the statement that those were boom times and that this was an inflated value. I am quite prepared to subscribe to that point of view. In this year of depression these same stocks represent a value of no less than $34,000,000; in other words the value of the stocks of the insurance companies held by the shareholders in Canada could be sold, on the present depressed market, for $34,000,000. I think it is fair to say that the main factor which determines the value of
a stock on the stock exchange is its earning power; there are other factors as well but the main factor is the earning power. As the stock was selling at too high a figure in 1928 I submit that it is selling at too low a figure to-day, because the earnings of the insurance companies are very small. Consequently the price has gone lower than the actual value. That price of $34,000,000 has no regard whatever to the equities behind these shares, so I will take an arbitrary figure of $50,000,000 as being certainly a fair figure though, probably too low, of the cost if we desired arbitrarily to take over the insurance companies in Canada.
At 4i per cent, which is the price we have to pay for money to-day, with that cost of $50,000,000, in order to break even we would require a revenue of $2,250,000 a year. As a matter of fact the total dividends paid to shareholders of Canadian companies last year was less than half that amount, so that upon the mere basis of dollars and cents we would be confronted immediately with two things. First we would be increasing the national debt by the sum I have indicated, and in addition we would be creating a yearly obligation in the form of interest which would require us to take more from the insurance policyholders than is being taken under private management.
In concluding his remarks my hon. friend said that we must make this nationalization compulsory. It may be that his advocacy of that policy came at the end of his speech, when' he was a bit hurried for time, but I noticed that he did nothing more than merely assert that this was what we should do. There are several questions I should like to put to my hon. friend. Assuming that it were desirable to take over the whole of the insurance business and it were wise to make insurance compulsory what would he do in the case of the man who says, " I cannot pay." Would he insure every adult over the age of twenty-one, without medical inspection and without regard to health? If he did so his cost of insurance would be infinitely more than it is to-day, because one of the reasons why the cost of insurance is kept at a low figure is the very careful selection made by the life insurance companies.
Just on that point let me say that my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Ger-shaw) put his finger upon one of the greatest services that is being rendered by the insurance companies. They do not by any means confine their activities to the endeavour to sell insurance in order to make a profit; they enter very largely into social service
*478
Lije Insurance-Mr. Rhodes

activities, which are of lasting benefit to the health of the people of the country, by their social service work, their support of public health institutions, public health education and control, especially with regard to maternal and infantile mortality and tuberculosis, and the provisions obtaining in many companies which call for medical inspection on the part of policyholders at stated periods.
To-day in Canada there are policies in effect, issued by Canadian life insurance companies, aggregating somewhere in the neighbourhood of seven thousand million dollars. That is the face value; I think I can find the exact figures here. The exact figure is $7,225,000,000; that is the face value of insurance policies issued by Canadian insurance companies, but of that sum only $4,300,000,000 is applicable to policies issued within the Dominion of Canada. The remainder, $2,900,000,000 represents the aggregate face value of policies issued in foreign countries. So I put this question to my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin:	If he is going to nationalize
the insurance business in Canada what is to be done with respect to the insurance business in foreign countries? Are we to lose that business? Certainly we cannot retain it unless we allow reciprocal rights to those in other countries to insure in Canada, because I may point out to my hon. friend that one-third of the total insurance business in Canada is done by companies in foreign countries. If my hon. friend does restrict Canadian insurance companies to the Canadian field he cuts off that business, and in doing so he limits that spread of which he spoke a while ago when he said that the more insurance policies issued and the larger number of people insured, the cheaper the insurance would be for the individual.
In that connection, lest I forget, let me point out that if he is going to take over the insurance business in Canada as a national undertaking, what is he going to do with that amount of insurance now held in Canada by foreign companies? If he takes it over he has to compensate, and if he compensates he has to make a further commitment in addition to the figures which I gave a short time ago.

speechtext: Probably the nearest example we can get concerning the efficiency of state life insurance as contrasted with that conducted by private companies is to be found in New Zealand. speechtext: The rates of the two systems in New Zealand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED SYSTEM OF NATIONAL COMPULSORY INSURANCE
speechtext:
Their rates must be
similar, otherwise the proportion of insurance conducted by the state would tend to increase, rather than diminish, with respect to the total volume of insurance in force. That thought leads me to say that insurance is a very peculiar business; I know of none other . comparable to it. It is a type of business that has to be sold. It is a commodity the selling of which requires intensive effort. I believe that fact is proven beyond doubt by the circumstances that where you find state and private companies competing the private company wins out on every occasion.
Answering the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) may I say that when the royal commission on insurance sat here in 1906 this very question was raised. I have before me a portion of the evidence given
by Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, who, at that time, was general manager of the Imperial Life Insurance Company. Perhaps it would not be amiss to read the whole of it, despite the fact that it is a fairly long paragraph.
I am afraid my views are not in accord with the views of most of my colleagues, but I Judge that they will give me credit for sincerity in holding the views I do upon that subject. I have endeavoured to consider this matter from a public standpoint strictly, and therefore believe that state insurance is practical under certain conditions. I believe that state insurance would have a most helpful effect in educating public opinion as to the merits and the necessity of life insurance, and thus incidentally prove of very great benefit to the life insurance companies of Canada. I believe that state insurance under a sound management would' be helpful in assisting the regular life officers in reducing their rate of expense, and also helpful in assisting in solving some of the other vexatious problems which they are constantly brought in contact with. I do not think that such a department would be antagonistic to the interest of the regular life insurance companies, but would rather Drove an adjunct to the propaganda of the popularizing of life insurance. I think it may be likened unto the Post Office Savings Department. The experience has been, I believe, that the Post Office Savings Department of Canada has rather helped the chartered banks, has assisted in popularizing the thrift and increased the savings accounts in the chartered banks of Canada. So for these reasons, and for some others, I believe that state life insurance would not be an evil, but a great blessing to the public of this country, and I believe that the field is broad enough and is growing, and is able to sustain not only a life insurance department but to sustain and to make even more prosperous the life insurance companies which are at present operating in this field.
And Mr. T. B. Macaulay of the Sun Life Insurance Company gave the following evidence on the same occasion:
Mr. Bradshaw's last remark covered nearly all I had to say on this matter, because my position is simply this: 1 have no objection in the world to the establishment of a state life insurance department if it is thought desirable. I quite agree with Mr. Bradshaw that if these different things that he speaks about, if such a department can be managed free from politics, if the management is given a free hand, if the investments are not put into government securities yielding very low rates of interest, but the same scale is exercised in selecting them as in the case of a regular life insurance company, and if all the other things that go to make a successful life insurance company are put into a government institution, I see no reason in the world why it should not be a first-class success. But even if it were a first-class success I do not think it would amount to anything better than another first-class company. That would be all that would result.
I might make some observations with respect to the government entering business.

Life Insurance-Mr. Rhodes

This is a matter to which I have given a great deal of attention, and I know the same applies to many hon. members of this house. There are certain activities, even in this country where the trend is to expect the government to do everything, which are peculiarly adaptable to government handling. On the other hand, there are many phases of business which the government is not equipped to handle. If there is one business more than any other business of a highly specialized character which the government cannot be equipped to handle, it is the life insurance business. I submit in all seriousness that if it were possible to take over the life insurance business, assuming that it could be conducted by the government as efficiently as it is conducted as a private enterprise-I do not admit that but I will assume it for the sake of argument - it would lose that driving force without which the business would not increase and prosper as has been the case under private management. This is one of the classes of business which the government ought not to engage in unless it does so in competition with private enterprise and obtains the benefit of the stimulus which comes from competition. Even then it loses out in competition with private business as has been proven by experience not only in New Zealand but in Canada. We might take the case of England where insurance was sold through the postoffice for a great number of years. This system was in force from 1864 but was abandoned in 1928. The insurance was sold at less than cost but the whole matter was the subject of an investigation in 1920 by a committee presided over by Lord Parmoor. That committee found that although the expenditure incurred in administration was low and the terms of insurance much more favourable than those offered by insurance companies, the number of applications for insurance was extremely small and the system could only be described as a failure, one reason for this being that the system was not competitive and did not adopt canvassing methods. In July, 1928. the select committee on estimates recommended that post office life insurance business should be discontinued. This goes to illustrate that where you do not have that driving power behind the seeking for business, which I submit you cannot have in a state insurance, if you do not fail, you certainly are not going to have that degree of success which obtains in the case of a private company.

The hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has asked me to say something further with respect to the compulsory aspect of this matter. I must say that I was rather amazed at the suggestion of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. I had not given thought to that phase of the matter but I think the queries which I put to him indicate what is in my mind. What machinery could the government adopt to compel an individual to pay for insurance, even assuming that he is physically fit and a proper subject for insurance? The most the government could do would be to put him in gaol if he did not pay and1 that only makes the second condition worse than the first. We not only do not get the amount of the premium which he owes but we are put to the expense of providing him with free board and lodging. Are we to insure every individual when he reaches the age of twenty-one without any reference to his physical condition ? If that be so, then we will have to take in the lame, the halt and the blind. Are we to enter upon a gigantic scheme of benevolence and not have the matter dealt with upon an actuarial basis? The other alternative is to have this insurance stand upon its own feet and make the premium at least sufficient to carry the "policy. In this case we would be confronted with such high premiums that no one would insure. This seems to me to be the obvious answer.
I appreciate that all my hon. friend asks for in his resolution is:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the advisability of nationalizing life insurance.
But I would not wish it to be thought that the government is prepared to consider the nationalizing of insurance. Therefore, this

Life Insurance-Mr. Spencer
resolution cannot be accepted by the house. It adopts a principle which, in my judgment, is unworkable. No public reason has been given why it should be introduced. We are being well served at the moment. On the one hand we have the benefit of private management, with the urge which must be behind private management if they are to make a success of a business of that character. On the other hand, we have the benefit of supervision which has been of a singularly high type. This may be because we have been served by one of the most efficient public servants with whom I have come in contact in the person of the Superintendent of Insurance. I do know that the manner in which he has conducted his inspection has caused the insurance department of the Dominion of Canada to be looked up to as a pattern and an example by other countries of the world. On a recent visit of mine to the United States I had the privilege of meeting the members of ithe life insurance presidents' association during their annual meeting in New York. I was struck with the flattering remarks made by all of those who were associated with the insurance industry of that country as to the character and method of our inspection.
I hope the house in its wisdom will reject this resolution.
Mr. HENRY E. SPENCER (Battle River): The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) does not seem to be enthusiastically in favour of the resolution before 'the house. I agree that we have reason to be proud of our insurance companies in that they have not collapsed under this crisis, but they may have been kept going simply because of the penalties they have taken out of the people who have been insured.
I was very glad to learn that the Minister of Finance is critical of the very high salaries that are being paid in the insurance world to-day, although he rather implied that if you got cheaper men they would not be worth anything at all. But when the enormous salaries that are being paid, as stated by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), are recalled, higher salaries perhaps than are being paid to any other executives, even such high executives of the United States government as were mentioned, and when it is realized that these salaries have been increased as the depression has deepened, I think it will be agreed that it is time we asked some questions about these enhanced salaries. I would point out to the Minister of Finance that it is not always right to say that if you 74726-31
pay a less salary you do not get the same service. For if I might refer to the minister's own last words, we have in the employ of the dominion government one of the most valuable men possibly in the insurance world. He is doing a most excellent work, and he is to-day getting only one-twentieth of some of the high salaries that have been mentioned on the floor of the house to-day. So it is not necessarily a case of paying very high salaries to get efficient business men. I would also point out that although the insurance companies have not failed, it has been due largely to the fact that we have most efficient civil servants looking after their integrity. It is only a few years ago, on December 1, 1931, that a special order in council had to be passed to enable insurance companies in Canada to value their securities above the market price. I know that this was not done possibly except for the sake of one insurance company, but all the insurance companies had to accept what was being done.
I would also refer to the fact that the general manager of that one particular company was getting, and I suppose he is getting today, no less a sum than S100,080, and in spite of that nice little salary his company was so badly managed that he had to write off not only millions but hundreds of millions in the value of its securities due to the fall in the value of common stocks owned by his company.
The minister also referred to the very low cost of Canadian insurance. I wonder if he really heard the figures that were given by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin who pointed out that in the years 1930, 1931 and 1932 lapsed policies amounted to $1,200,000,000 and surrendered policies which people could not continue ito carry to no less a sum than $787,000,000. Surely there is something wrong with our life insurance business when over two billions of dollars of insurance has to be dropped in the course of a few years. Does that not show, as the mover of the resolution very well pointed out, that life insurance is too expensive. It is too expensive partly because of the enormous amount of overlapping. I understand that to get the first premium it costs, according to the figures given, anything from 48 to 75 per cent of the amount of the first premium.
The Minister of Finance started out and tried to build up a case against state life insurance, but he certainly cannot say with the short term insurance we have to-day, even though no insurance company may have failed, that we are giving the people of Canada

I should like to give some time to this resolution, Mr. Speaker, but owing to the fact that I have a resolution to follow immediately, I shall have to give the resolution of my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) the minimum of attention in order that I can give the maximum to my own, interested as I am in insurance.
My remarks on the resolution now before us are based on certain statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). He predicates his remarks on individual initiative, and also on the rights of private property. He began his speech by stating that he was proud of insurance as it is being conducted to-day in Canada by the private companies, but I would point out that the point is not so much whether we are proud of the present insurance system as run by private individuals in this country as it is a question whether the business could not be more effectively and efficiently and cheaply run by the state.
The Minister of Finance instanced insurance in the civil service as a criterion by which we could judge the business of insurance if controlled by the state, but he gave no facts or conditions whatsoever in regard to that, and therefore in this house at least to-day we are not in a position to measure what success state insurance would have as judged by insurance as it is being carried on in the civil service to-day.

The minister also said that the present day insurance companies are doing everything possible to prolong the life of their policyholders. But it seems to me that insurance as it is controlled to-day by private enterprise is more interested in the financial health of the shareholders thereof than in the health of the policy-holders. Only two years ago the government had to come as a sort of physician to the rescue to save insurance companies through an order in council by pegging their shares, that is, by striking an average price over five different periods. If the minister predicates his statement on private enterprise, I might say that the state meanwhile has usually shown far greater solicitude for the rights of property than for the rights of man. Joseph Chamberlain made this statement some years ago:
The rights of property have been so much extended that the rights of the community have almost altogether disappeared, and it is hardly too much to say that the prosperity and comfort and the liberties of a great proportion of the population have been laid at the feet of .a small number of proprietors, who neither toil nor spin.
Most of those shareholders surely are in the position of those who neither toil nor spin. Certainly a great deal of the exorbitant profits which they have made have not been earned through any excessive toiling or spinning. Mr. I/ewis, another authority on insurance, has this to say in regard to state insurance control:
The state should move cautiously and tentatively in the direction of experiment; but, as the evolution of the modern state plainly shows, must move. It must often subordinate the independence of the individual to the general good; it must work out many of its beneficent purposes by collective means; it must sometimes compel the individual to do that which he ought to be willing to do.
I maintain that nothing said in the house to-day Aows that insurance could not be efficiently and effectively carried on by the state. Notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has said that the insurance business is too intricate to be carried on by the state, I still hold that it is possible for the state to cany on insurance very efficiently and effectively. It is no great mystery; the business of insurance in both this country and all others is to-day the safest I know. The application of the insurance principle, in my opinion, presents no great difficulties or risks. It is not, as has been suggested, some venture upon unknown seas; it is the safest business in the whole world. It as not as complex as the Minister

Life Insurance-Mr. Irvine
of Finance would have this house believe. Therefore, I think for the state to assume the business of insurance would not involve its entering upon any new untried and dangerous ground. Insurance under government operation would be purely mutual, and if it should be administered on a basis of profits, the profits would certainly go to the state treasury rather than to the pockets of shareholders of private companies as is 'the practice at present. State ownership would prevent the system of interlocking directorship which we have in this country at the present time and through the instrumentality of which 8200,000,000 in worthless shares have been thrown upon the present insurance companies to the detriment of the policyholders thereof.
The first and fundamental principle of insurance is mutuality, the principle of each for all and all for each. Doctor Gerhart has said this in regard to insurance control by the state:
All human progress which is essentially an increase in social well-being has arisen from some improved method of cooperation, whether this new form of cooperation has resulted from private initiative or from public compulsion in obedience to enacted law. There is probably no other form of cooperation which is so fundamentally valuable to the cooperative members, indiscriminately, rather than particular members, than insurance.
In insurance is found every essence of cooperation. If that is so, I hold that any cooperative movement would be more successful, controlled by the state than it is at the present time, controlled by private individuals. In Italy there is a criterion by which we can judge state insurance. They have a monopoly of insurance there; by the Italian law of 1912 insurance in that country has been made a state monopoly. The issue of all policies of life insurance is entrusted to a national institute of insurance, a department of the state to which the state treasury issues the money necessary for its operations and whatever profit results does not go to the normal expenses of the state but is set aside in toto for the specific social purpose of providing pensions for workingmen.
Switzerland also provides for state monopoly of insurance, especially in the case of accidents and sickness. New Zealand at the present time has a system of state insurance, although competition of private companies is allowed there. I believe, fundamentally, scientifically and mathematically, state control of insurance is advisable, practicable and possible. If we had state insurance it would certainly aid the Minister of Finance in financ-74726-31J
ing the affairs of Canada more efficiently than is being done at the present time. Bonds could be sold to these insurance companies and I do not see why investments should not be limited to government bonds rather than allow the managers, presidents, administrations of the present concerns to gamble in all kinds of worthless shares and even in all sorts of worthless mortgages. In insurance as it is being carried on to-day by private concerns, there is too much overhead, too much overlapping, too many agency branches overlapping throughout the country. It has been suggested that if insurance were made a government monopoly, this would entail the confiscation of the buildings of these private concerns, but in Edmonton most of the buildings in which these insurance companies do their business do not belong to the companies; they are rented, and most of the business in Ottawa is also done in rented buildings. It is only at headquarters in Toronto and similar places that they actually own their buildings.
I shall conclude with the remark that under state supervision of insurance the families and the policyholders would be better safeguarded than they are now under privately owned insurance companies.

I am glad to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a great deal to which to reply. Not much objection has been taken to the resolution, and the arguments of those who did take objection were not effective. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), was the chief objector to the motion. He, speaking for the government of course, says the government will not let it be thought that they are willing even to consider such a resolution. Let me say to my hon. friend that the government might better consider it. Let me also say that it is only too obvious that so far the government have not considered it. This is not a question that can be thrown aside with that suggestion of untouchability. I hope my hon. friend will not take that attitude with regard to other matters of this sort. The government has a duty to consider whether the people of Canada can get safer and cheaper life insurance through government ownership and control than through private companies
The Minister of Finance says that while I stated that life insurance companies in Canada are perhaps as good as those in any other country, I suggested the contrary, when I quoted findings with regard to insurance companies in New York and pointed out that the same might be true of some companies in
Lije Insurance-Mr. Irvine

Canada. When I say that Canadian companies are as safe and as efficiently managed as any others I also say that they are not any better managed or any more efficient than companies in other parts of the world. So when we find certain conditions in connection with well-managed and safe companies in New York it is reasonable to suppose that you could find pretty much the same thing in regard to Canadian companies, particularly when some of those New York companies are doing business in Canada.
The minister also said there was no criticism to be made about high salaries in Canada. Again I want to tell him that some of the companies to which I referred do business in Canada. And may I suggest to him that I know there are managers of insurance companies in Canada getting salaries they are incapable of earning, and they can do that only at the expense of the policyholders.
The minister dealt with the liabilities involved, but I am bound to say that I know no more about the liabilities involved than I did before the minister started. No doubt that is my fault, but so far as I am concerned his presentation was so utterly confusing that I was not able to follow it. I would say that if the liabilities have to be taken over and met in the way the Minister of Finance tried to describe I am sure this is not the government to do it; we will have to wait until we get some other government, for apparently there is not the knowledge of insurance or the appreciation of its importance to the average citizen that we would expect from a government that could be expected to handle adequately a business of that sort.
With regard to the compulsory feature, the Minister of Finance thinks he has knocked my whole argument into a cocked hat when he asks: What would you do with a man who could not or would not pay his premium? Well, what do you do with anybody who does not obey the law of the country? There must be punishment of some sort. What is done now? When a man cannot pay the premium charged by private companies, and dies leaving his children starving, what do we do? The community takes care of his children and feeds them, whether it be the municipality or the provincial government. So it could not be any worse under compulsory insurance. But I am quite sure that if the minister turned that great mind which he undoubtedly possesses to the simple little problem of what to do with a man who refuses to pay his premium under a compulsory system he could find some way of dealing with the matter. I believe I could.

Then he says: Are we to look after the lame, the halt, and the blind? What else is insurance for? What does my hon. friend suppose it is for? Would he look after the strong and those who can foresee everything? Such people do not need to be looked after. It is the very essence of insurance that it takes care of the lame, the halt and the blind; if it does not do that it is not worth having. As I pointed out, we, as a nation, have to do that already whether we go into the insurance business or not. Having then to do it for those who cannot pay anything at all surety we should not allow private companies to skim the cream by taking the business of people who can pay and leaving the state to carry those who cannot.
Then as to what is to be done with the insurance business in foreign countries, are we as a nation to go into foreign countries to do business? No, let us mind our own business. Our business is to insure the people of Canada. We are not interested in trying to insure Americans and the people in other countries; we will let them look after their own business.
Then the minister said that in New Zealand they have private companies operating in competition with government insurance, and if I got his figures correctly I think they were to the advantage of the private companies.
